title: Lesson 1: Correlation
text:
1.1 Pearson, Spearman and Kendall

Pearson’s correlation summarises a linear relationship between two continuous variables.
Spearman’s rank correlation summarises a monotonic relationship using ranks.
Kendall’s tau is another rank-based measure useful with ordinal data or many ties.

The coefficient of determination is \(r^2\). It is the squared correlation, not the percentage of one variable literally caused by another.

title: Lesson 1: Correlation
text:

Confirm that age and trestbps are continuous.
Select Analyses > Exploration > Descriptives.
Add age and trestbps to Variables.
Request descriptive statistics, histograms, Q-Q plots and boxplots.
Describe the centre, spread, shape and unusual observations.

title: Lesson 1: Correlation
text:
2.3 Calculate the correlation

Select Analyses > Regression > Correlation Matrix.
Add age and trestbps.
Select Spearman to reproduce the source workflow. Optionally display Pearson for comparison.
Request the significance level, confidence interval if available, and a plot if supported.







NoteTeaching note



The source uses Shapiro-Wilk tests to select Pearson or Spearman correlation. If retained, also emphasise the scatterplot and form of the relationship. A formal normality test can flag small departures that are not practically important.

2.4 Interpret the result

There was a [weak/moderate/strong] [positive/negative] association between age and resting systolic blood pressure, Spearman’s \(r_s\) = [value], 95% CI [lower, upper], \(p\) = [value].

text: Workshop home | Previous: Correlation

title: Lesson 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
1.1 Hypothesis test
\[H_0:b=0 \qquad H_1:b\ne0\]
The p-value assesses compatibility with a zero slope under the model assumptions. The confidence interval expresses uncertainty in the coefficient.

title: Lesson 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
1.2 Model fit

\(R^2\) is the proportion of observed outcome variance accounted for by the fitted model in the sample.
Adjusted \(R^2\) penalises model complexity and is helpful when comparing models with different numbers of predictors.

title: Lesson 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.1 Interpret the source result
The source reports \(R=0.315\), adjusted \(R^2=0.09\), an age coefficient of 0.604 mmHg per year and a 95% confidence interval of approximately 0.24 to 0.97. Verify all values in jamovi.

For each additional year of age, mean resting SBP was estimated to change by [coefficient] mmHg (95% CI [lower, upper], \(p\) = [value]). The model accounted for [R-squared x 100]% of sample variance in resting SBP.

title: Lesson 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.2 Confidence and prediction intervals
A confidence interval around the fitted mean describes uncertainty in the estimated mean outcome. A prediction interval describes where a new individual observation may fall and is therefore wider.

title: Lesson 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.3 Assumptions and diagnostics

Outcome type: trestbps is continuous.
Linearity: residuals should show no systematic curve against fitted values.
Homoscedasticity: residual spread should be reasonably consistent across fitted values.
Residual normality: the Q-Q plot should show no serious systematic departures.
Independence: justify this from study design and sampling, not merely a plot.
Influence: inspect Cook’s distance and investigate influential cases.







CautionCorrection to the source slides



A random-looking residual plot does not prove independence. Also avoid treating 10 or 20 observations per predictor as a universal minimum; required sample size depends on precision, complexity, effect sizes and data quality.

title: Lesson 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
1.1 Multicollinearity
Strong relationships among predictors can make coefficients unstable. Inspect VIFs, tolerance, the correlation matrix and coefficient uncertainty. VIF < 5 is only a rule of thumb.

title: Lesson 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
1.2 Overfitting and model selection
A model can fit the present sample while performing poorly on new data. Avoid presenting automated stepwise selection as the default. Prefer predictors chosen from the research question and subject knowledge, with validation or penalised methods when prediction is the goal.






WarningDecision for instructor review



The source teaches stepwise selection. This lesson preserves it as an optional legacy workflow, but it should be reviewed by the statistics instructors.

title: Lesson 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
2.1 Recommended workflow: prespecified model

State the model and rationale before inspecting p-values.
Confirm measurement levels and reference categories.
Examine missing data and distributions.
Examine relationships among continuous predictors.
Put trestbps in Dependent Variable.
Put continuous predictors such as age, chol and thalach in Covariates.
Put categorical predictors such as sex and fbs in Factors.
Request model fit, coefficient confidence intervals, residual plots, a Q-Q plot, collinearity statistics and Cook’s distance.
Interpret the model, uncertainty and diagnostics.

2.3 Reporting template

The model included [predictors] and accounted for [adjusted R-squared x 100]% of sample variance in resting SBP. Holding other predictors constant, [predictor] was associated with an estimated [coefficient] mmHg change per [unit/category contrast] (95% CI [lower, upper], \(p\) = [value]). Diagnostics showed [description].

title: Lesson 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
2.4 Model checklist
Record the outcome and predictors, measurement levels, reference categories, model equation, coefficient estimates, confidence intervals, \(R^2\), adjusted \(R^2\), residual diagnostics, influential observations, limitations and plain-language conclusion.
